title: REE: A Scientific Research Entrance Exam for AI Agents

Title:REE: A Scientific Research Entrance Exam for AI Agents
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Autonomous research agents are emerging as a promising approach to scientific problem-solving across disciplines, owing to their growing ability to improve a solution through repeated experiments. Evaluating this ability requires benchmarks that pose open-ended research problems and measure improvements over established scientific methods. We introduce REE (Research Entrance Exam), a benchmark that tests AI agents on scientific research. It consists of 100 open-ended research problems spanning five broad scientific areas and 23 domains. To ensure high quality, every problem is drawn from active research in its field and individually reviewed by domain experts. Each problem is posed as a task of iterative improvement: an agent has up to 12 hours to improve a working starter solution, and REE scores the result on a common scale against an established expert solution evaluated under comparable conditions. By this measure, two of the four frontier agents we evaluate, Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol, outperform the expert solutions on 86% and 81% of problems, across all five scientific areas. Their runs also show how they do so: both agents surpass the expert solutions within the first two hours on average, and their best solutions mostly tailor or combine established methods of the field. REE thus provides a unified framework for evaluating autonomous scientific research, capturing both improvements over established methods and the research processes behind them.

report.summary: REE is a new 100-problem benchmark that tests autonomous AI research agents on improving expert starter solutions across 23 scientific domains.
report.background: Autonomous research agents are moving from coding and question-answering tasks toward open-ended scientific problem-solving. Most existing AI benchmarks measure closed-form answers, short tasks, or code generation, but they do not capture whether an agent can iteratively improve a working solution over hours and beat established expert methods. REE was built to fill that gap. It draws 100 open-ended problems from active research across five scientific areas and 23 domains, with each problem reviewed by domain experts. Agents get up to 12 hours to improve a starter solution, and results are scored on a common scale against an expert solution evaluated under comparable conditions. This makes REE less a knowledge quiz and more a research-process stress test.
key_points: REE contains 100 open-ended research problems spanning five scientific areas and 23 domains. Each problem comes from active research and is individually reviewed by domain experts, then posed as an iterative improvement task with up to 12 hours of agent work.

Two of four evaluated frontier agents outperform expert solutions: Claude Opus 5.5 on 86% of problems and GPT-6.1 Sol on 81%, across all five scientific areas. The benchmark thus reports a striking headline result for long-horizon research agents.

The agents often surpass expert solutions within the first two hours on average. Their best solutions mostly tailor or combine established methods in the field rather than producing entirely new scientific ideas.

REE scores final solutions against expert baselines under comparable conditions and also examines the research process. This gives a unified framework for measuring both improvement over established methods and how agents achieve it.
report.impact: For the AI industry, REE shifts evaluation from static knowledge and coding tests toward long-horizon, open-ended research tasks with expert baselines. That could push labs to optimize agent persistence, experiment design, tool use, and reproducibility rather than single-shot answers. For developers, it signals demand for robust agent harnesses, sandboxed compute, experiment tracking, and expert-review pipelines. For regular users, the results suggest AI research assistants may soon speed up technical work, but the finding that agents mainly recombine established methods should temper claims of fully autonomous scientific discovery. Benchmark overfitting, baseline comparability, and expert-review cost remain key concerns.
report.tools: Start with the REE paper on arXiv and watch for released code, task definitions, and scoring protocols. Related evaluation harnesses include Inspect, HELM, and lm-evaluation-harness; agent frameworks worth monitoring include AutoGen, LangGraph, and OpenHands. For reproducibility, use Docker, DVC, and W&B. Compare REE with related benchmarks such as ScienceAgentBench and MLAgentBench, and inspect expert-baseline conditions before citing leaderboard results.
